scenes.narration: A quick recap. On Sunday, November eighth, Jensen Huang, Nvidia's founder and chief executive, sent an email to employees. In it he wrote, I was unfaithful to my wife. The same day, the board opened an independent investigation, in light of reporting that he had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The New York Times and the Financial Times had reported that American officials believed a businesswoman linked to an Nvidia customer was working for China's intelligence service. China called that unsubstantiated, and nobody has been charged.

scenes.narration: Wednesday had started as a good day. Then, a little before five in the afternoon, the second story broke.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: On Wednesday, November eleventh, the New York Times reported that Huang had had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia vice president who reports to him. The Times cited five people who had worked at the company. According to the report, both were married to other people.

Here is what is not confirmed. Huang has not confirmed it. Nvidia has not commented. NBC News said it had not confirmed the Times report. When the Times reached Huang by phone, he said, I don't think you should be talking to me directly. We are not naming the executive, and we will not speculate about her. She is not accused of anything.

So why would this matter to investors at all? Because of the reporting line. A chief executive in a relationship with someone who reports to him is not a gossip question for a board. It is a governance question, about conflicts of interest and about who knew what. That is the lens the market used.

scenes.narration: The timing shows it. Nvidia's shares had actually closed up two point eight six percent on Wednesday, at about a hundred and seventy-four dollars. In trading after the close, they slid. By about five twenty-five in the evening, New York time, the price had touched about a hundred and fifty-six dollars, roughly ten percent below the close. At eight in the evening, the last after-hours trade was still about a hundred and fifty-nine dollars. On Thursday morning, before the open, rivals AMD and Broadcom were up, and Nvidia was still down nearly eight percent.

scenes.narration: And while the price was falling, the board was meeting.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia's board was preparing to oust Huang. Semafor reported the same, and added that the full board had yet to make a decision. CNBC confirmed that the board met on Wednesday to discuss whether to remove him. On Thursday morning, CNBC wrote that no outcome had been announced.

Notice the contrast with four days earlier. On Sunday, the board's own statement said it had confidence in Jensen and his leadership team. As of Thursday morning, that line had not been withdrawn or updated in public. There was no new statement on the company's newsroom, and no new filing with the SEC. Everything about a possible change of leadership was still coming from reporting, not from Nvidia.

Bloomberg reported that Nvidia was working with an outside search firm to identify chief executive candidates, and was weighing an interim leader first. Semafor reported that some directors favor the chief financial officer, Colette Kress, for that interim role. Those are reports. No name has been confirmed by the company.

Could a board really remove the founder of a company like this? According to Nvidia's latest proxy statement, Huang owns about three point six percent of the company's shares, mostly through family trusts. That is a fortune, but it is far from a majority. The chief executive serves at the pleasure of the board, which CNBC says has eleven directors and a lead director instead of a chair. And removing him as chief executive would not, by itself, remove him from the board. And the proxy statement does not use the word succession even once.

Let me draw the decision. Here is the board. Here is the chief executive's seat. The board appoints whoever sits in it. Today that arrow points at the founder. If the board changes its mind, the arrow moves to an interim leader, while a search firm looks for a permanent one. And by law, the company would have to tell regulators, normally within four business days.

scenes.narration: Meanwhile, in Washington, the reaction was getting louder.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Senator Kevin Cramer, a Republican from North Dakota, told Politico that the potential for extortion was so tremendous, given something as sensitive as Nvidia chips, that, in his words, he's got to go. Representative Suhas Subramanyam, a Democrat from Virginia, told CNBC that Huang should resign. Those are their opinions. No regulator has made a finding.

Two House committee chairmen, Brian Mast and John Moolenaar, said they had not heard from Huang and gave him until the end of Wednesday to respond. Asked whether subpoenas were possible, Mast said, yes.

In the Senate, Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons asked the Commerce Department to preserve its records on Nvidia's chip exports to China, writing that the incident raises significant concerns about the government's ability to enforce export controls. And in January, Democrats take control of both chambers, with the power to issue subpoenas.

scenes.narration: So what is the market actually pricing?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Remember the phrase from our last video, key person risk. Nvidia's annual report says it is highly dependent on its longstanding executive team. The analyst Stacy Rasgon summed it up in five words. Jensen is Nvidia. Nvidia is Jensen.

Some analysts have put numbers on that. Dan Ives said that if Huang were removed, Nvidia would be worth a lot less, twenty-five to thirty percent, and he gave different price targets depending on whether Huang stays or goes. Bernstein downgraded the stock and cut its target in half. Those are opinions, not facts. But they show how a single seat can move a valuation by hundreds of billions of dollars.

And look at the neighbors. When Nvidia fell, AMD and Broadcom rose, on Monday and again on Thursday morning. Investors were not selling chips. They were selling uncertainty about one company's leadership, and buying its rivals.

scenes.narration: Which leaves three things to watch.

scenes.narration: Let me draw them. First, the board. Any decision about the chief executive should show up in a filing with the SEC. Second, the results. Nvidia is scheduled to report on November seventeenth. Third, Congress. House chairmen have asked for a closed-door briefing on November eighteenth, and it is still not confirmed. All three arrows point at the same question, who runs Nvidia.

As of a little after eight in the morning, New York time, on Thursday, November twelfth, before the market opened, Nvidia's board had not announced a decision. There was no new filing with regulators and no new statement from Huang. If the board does act, the company would normally have to disclose it within four business days, so that filing is the first thing to look for.

scenes.narration: So why is Nvidia worth so much less than a week ago? Not because its chips changed. Because investors are trying to price a company that, by its own admission, depends heavily on its leaders, at the exact moment its board is reported to be debating whether to replace the most important one. Nothing in this story has been proven in court, and nobody has been charged. But markets do not wait for verdicts. They price people, and they price uncertainty. And for now, the biggest uncertainty in artificial intelligence is not a chip. It is a chair.
